result:
There is something quietly miraculous about ordinary mornings. The world does not announce itself with trumpets; it arrives in small, repeatable gestures. A kettle begins to murmur. Light finds the edge of a table. Someone, somewhere, opens a curtain and discovers that the day has already been waiting.

I have always been drawn to the way small things carry disproportionate meaning. A well-worn book says not only that it has been read, but that it has accompanied a life through weather, boredom, grief, and moments of attention. A chipped mug is not just damaged; it is familiar. A street tree, stubbornly growing through a crack in the pavement, becomes a declaration that softness can persist inside hard places.

People often imagine wonder as a rare event, but I suspect it is more like a practice. It lives in noticing. The first sip of coffee. The sound of rain on a roof. The fact that language, with a little patience, can move one private mind into another. Even our misunderstandings are proof of something astonishing: we are trying, constantly, to translate ourselves.

And perhaps that is the central task of being alive—translation. Turning feeling into words, memory into story, intention into action, loneliness into company. We do it imperfectly. We leave meaning half-finished. But there is grace in the attempt.

So much of life is not grand, not polished, not resolved. Yet it is still worth attending to. The ordinary is not a lesser category of existence. It is the place where existence actually happens.
